options.a: Short-term, high-quality debt instruments
options.b: Long-term, investment-grade corporate notes
options.c: Short-term, high-yield corporate bonds
options.d: Exchange-traded funds holding T-notes

distractorExplanations.b: Long-term notes are capital-market instruments; money market paper matures within about a year.
distractorExplanations.c: Money market instruments are high quality; high-yield debt is not.
distractorExplanations.d: An ETF is a fund, not a money market instrument, and T-notes run 2–10 years.

options.a: The insurer, through its general account
options.b: The separate account's portfolio manager
options.c: The insurer for all subaccount losses
options.d: The contract owner, through subaccounts

distractorExplanations.a: General-account guarantees back fixed annuities, not variable subaccount returns.
distractorExplanations.b: Managers run the subaccounts but do not absorb investment losses.
distractorExplanations.c: The insurer bears investment risk only on fixed or guaranteed riders, not subaccount returns.

options.a: Credit risk of a bond's issuer
options.b: Time remaining until a bond matures
options.c: A stock's sensitivity to the market
options.d: Bond price sensitivity to rate changes

distractorExplanations.a: Credit risk is measured by ratings and spreads, not duration.
distractorExplanations.b: Maturity is a date; duration weights the timing of all cash flows.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensitivity of a stock to the market is beta.

options.a: A foreign share traded on its home exchange
options.b: A U.S. company's shares sold to foreign buyers
options.c: A fund that holds a basket of foreign stocks
options.d: A U.S.-traded receipt for foreign company shares

distractorExplanations.a: An ADR trades in the U.S., not on the foreign home exchange.
distractorExplanations.b: ADRs represent foreign issuers' shares, not U.S. companies'.
distractorExplanations.c: A basket of foreign stocks is a fund, while an ADR represents one issuer.

options.a: Reinvestment risk if called when rates fall
options.b: Default risk if called when rates rise
options.c: Liquidity risk because they cannot be sold
options.d: Inflation risk because coupons adjust to CPI

distractorExplanations.b: Issuers call bonds when rates fall, not when they rise, and calling is not default.
distractorExplanations.c: Callable bonds trade in the secondary market like other bonds.
distractorExplanations.d: Callable bond coupons are fixed; CPI-adjusted coupons describe TIPS.

options.a: Daily liquidity and SEC registration as investment companies
options.b: Lower fees and restrictions on leverage and short selling
options.c: Flexible strategies, higher fees, and investor eligibility limits
options.d: Open availability to retail investors with low investment minimums

distractorExplanations.a: Hedge funds usually limit redemptions and rely on exemptions from Investment Company Act registration.
distractorExplanations.b: Hedge funds typically charge more and may use leverage and shorting freely.
distractorExplanations.d: Hedge funds are usually limited to accredited or qualified investors with high minimums.

options.a: Professional management and diversification
options.b: Guaranteed principal backed by the fund sponsor
options.c: Intraday trading at prices set by the market
options.d: Direct voting control over each underlying stock

distractorExplanations.b: Mutual funds do not guarantee principal; share values fluctuate.
distractorExplanations.c: Mutual funds are priced once daily at NAV; intraday trading describes ETFs.
distractorExplanations.d: The fund votes proxies for its holdings, not individual shareholders.

options.a: Are priced once a day at net asset value
options.b: Trade intraday on exchanges at market prices
options.c: Are always actively managed by a portfolio team
options.d: Are redeemed directly with the issuing fund

distractorExplanations.a: Once-daily NAV pricing describes open-end mutual funds.
distractorExplanations.c: Most ETFs track indexes; active ETFs exist but are not the rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Retail investors sell ETF shares on an exchange; only authorized participants redeem with the fund.

options.a: Rising interest rates lowering prices
options.b: Default by the U.S. Treasury as issuer
options.c: Reinvestment of coupons at lower rates
options.d: Inflation eroding purchasing power

distractorExplanations.a: TIPS prices still fall when real rates rise; they do not remove interest-rate risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Default risk on Treasuries is minimal; TIPS are designed for inflation.
distractorExplanations.c: Reinvestment risk still applies to TIPS coupons.

options.a: Sell the stock at the strike before expiration
options.b: Buy the stock at the strike before expiration
options.c: Buy the stock at the strike only at expiration
options.d: Sell the stock at market price at expiration

distractorExplanations.a: The right to sell at the strike belongs to a put buyer.
distractorExplanations.c: Exercise only at expiration describes European-style options.
distractorExplanations.d: A call gives a right to buy at the strike, not to sell at market.

options.a: Lower credit risk and usually lower yields
options.b: Higher credit risk and usually higher yields
options.c: Lower credit risk and usually higher yields
options.d: Equal credit risk but longer maturities

distractorExplanations.b: Higher credit risk and yields describe junk (high-yield) bonds.
distractorExplanations.c: Investors accept lower yields for lower credit risk, not higher.
distractorExplanations.d: Ratings reflect different credit risk; maturity is not the distinction.

options.a: Semiannual coupon payments at a fixed rate
options.b: Interest paid in a lump sum each year
options.c: Price gains from falling rates only
options.d: Accretion from discount to face value

distractorExplanations.a: Zero-coupon bonds pay no periodic coupons.
distractorExplanations.b: Zeros make no annual payments; all return comes at maturity or sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Rate changes affect price, but the built-in return is the accreting discount.

options.a: Mortgage loans insured by federal agencies
options.b: Real estate cash flows via a pooled security
options.c: Direct ownership of a single rental property
options.d: Construction loans made to homebuilders

distractorExplanations.a: Agency-insured mortgages describe GNMA pass-throughs, not REITs.
distractorExplanations.c: REIT holders own shares in a portfolio, not title to a property.
distractorExplanations.d: Some mortgage REITs lend, but REITs mainly give pooled real estate exposure.

options.a: Gets dividend priority over common, with limited votes
options.b: Has voting rights but is paid after common holders
options.c: Pays variable dividends that rise with earnings
options.d: Has priority over bonds in a corporate liquidation

distractorExplanations.b: Preferred holders are paid before common and usually cannot vote.
distractorExplanations.c: Preferred dividends are usually fixed; common dividends vary with earnings.
distractorExplanations.d: Bondholders are paid before preferred holders in liquidation.

options.a: Buys more of the best performers to add momentum
options.b: Changes target weights to follow market trends
options.c: Moves the full portfolio to cash after losses
options.d: Sells winners and buys laggards to reset targets

distractorExplanations.a: Adding to winners increases drift from targets, the opposite of rebalancing.
distractorExplanations.b: Rebalancing restores existing targets; it does not chase trends.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving to cash after losses is market timing, not rebalancing.

options.a: Hold winning positions too long before selling
options.b: Feel losses more strongly than equal gains
options.c: Overweight recent news when forecasting prices
options.d: Anchor to the price they originally paid

distractorExplanations.a: Loss aversion leads investors to sell winners early and hold losers.
distractorExplanations.c: Overweighting recent events is recency bias.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixing on a purchase price is anchoring.

options.a: Actively managed funds with high turnover
options.b: Taxable bond funds paying monthly interest
options.c: Low-turnover index equity funds
options.d: Short-term trading to harvest small gains

distractorExplanations.a: High turnover generates frequent taxable capital gains distributions.
distractorExplanations.b: Bond interest is taxed as ordinary income each year.
distractorExplanations.d: Short-term gains are taxed at higher ordinary income rates.

options.a: Choosing the lowest-cost options regardless of quality
options.b: Following the plan sponsor's directions in all cases
options.c: Guaranteeing participants against any investment loss
options.d: Acting solely in the interest of plan participants

distractorExplanations.a: ERISA requires prudence; cost matters, but lowest cost alone is not the standard.
distractorExplanations.b: Fiduciaries must not follow directions that conflict with participants' interests.
distractorExplanations.c: ERISA requires prudence and diversification, not loss guarantees.

options.a: Put the client's interests ahead of its own
options.b: Recommend only products that are suitable
options.c: Disclose conflicts only when clients ask
options.d: Seek the lowest-cost product in all cases

distractorExplanations.b: Suitability is a lower standard than the fiduciary duty of loyalty.
distractorExplanations.c: Fiduciaries must disclose material conflicts proactively.
distractorExplanations.d: Cost matters, but fiduciary duty weighs all factors, not only price.

options.a: A mostly bond portfolio to protect principal
options.b: Equal weights in stocks, bonds, and cash
options.c: Mostly money market funds for liquidity
options.d: A higher equity allocation than a retiree

distractorExplanations.a: A long horizon and high tolerance allow more equity exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: An equal split is more conservative than this profile needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavy cash sacrifices growth over a long horizon.

options.a: Municipal bonds inside a traditional IRA
options.b: Tax-efficient index funds in tax-deferred accounts
options.c: Tax-inefficient assets in tax-advantaged accounts
options.d: High-yield bonds in a taxable brokerage account

distractorExplanations.a: Munis are already tax-exempt, so holding them in an IRA wastes the benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Tax-efficient index funds usually belong in taxable accounts.
distractorExplanations.d: High-yield bond interest is taxed as ordinary income, so it fits better in tax-advantaged accounts.

options.a: Roth IRAs of the original owner after age 73
options.b: Taxable brokerage accounts after retirement
options.c: 529 plans once the beneficiary turns 18
options.d: Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s after RMD age

distractorExplanations.a: Original Roth IRA owners have no RMDs.
distractorExplanations.b: Taxable accounts have no required distributions.
distractorExplanations.c: 529 plans have no required distributions.

options.a: Specific securities to buy each quarter
options.b: Goals, constraints, risk, and allocation
options.c: A projected return target for each year
options.d: The adviser's fee schedule and billing

distractorExplanations.a: An IPS sets policy and ranges, not a list of trades.
distractorExplanations.c: An IPS may state a required return, but not a promised annual target.
distractorExplanations.d: Fees belong in the advisory agreement and Form ADV.

options.a: Investing a lump sum when prices look low
options.b: Buying the same number of shares each month
options.c: Investing a fixed dollar amount at intervals
options.d: Selling a fixed dollar amount each month

distractorExplanations.a: Buying on perceived lows is market timing.
distractorExplanations.b: A fixed share count is not dollar-cost averaging; the dollar amount is fixed.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixed withdrawals are a systematic withdrawal plan.

options.a: Growth stocks for a higher expected return
options.b: Long-term bonds to lock in a higher yield
options.c: Capital preservation and liquidity
options.d: A balanced fund of stocks and bonds

distractorExplanations.a: Stocks can fall sharply within a year.
distractorExplanations.b: Long bonds can lose value if rates rise before the purchase.
distractorExplanations.d: A balanced fund still carries meaningful equity risk over 12 months.

options.a: Reduce unsystematic risk through low correlation
options.b: Remove market risk by holding many securities
options.c: Raise expected return without adding risk
options.d: Replace the need to set an asset allocation

distractorExplanations.b: Market (systematic) risk cannot be diversified away.
distractorExplanations.c: Diversification improves risk-adjusted return but does not raise return for free.
distractorExplanations.d: Diversification works within an allocation; it does not replace one.

options.a: The client's age as the single deciding factor
options.b: The client's past returns in other accounts
options.c: The risk level of the adviser's model portfolio
options.d: Willingness and ability to take risk, plus goals

distractorExplanations.a: Age matters, but it is only one input.
distractorExplanations.b: Past returns do not show willingness or capacity to bear losses.
distractorExplanations.c: The model's risk describes the product, not the client.

series-66-readiness-check-recommendation.prompt: When assessing a client's risk tolerance, an adviser should consider:

options.a: Everyone pays the same percentage of income
options.b: Tax rates fall as taxable income rises
options.c: Marginal rates rise as taxable income rises
options.d: Taxes are based on spending, not income

distractorExplanations.a: One rate for all income levels is a flat tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Falling rates as income rises is a regressive system.
distractorExplanations.d: Taxes on spending are consumption taxes, such as sales taxes.

options.a: Are banned in all adviser advertising
options.b: May be used without any disclosures
options.c: May be used if disclosures are met
options.d: Are allowed only for hedge fund ads

distractorExplanations.a: The 2020 marketing rule lifted the outright ban.
distractorExplanations.b: Testimonials require disclosures, such as whether the person was paid.
distractorExplanations.d: The rule applies to all SEC-registered advisers, not only hedge funds.

options.a: Disclosed only if the client asks about it
options.b: Avoided entirely by refusing any compensation
options.c: Identified, disclosed, and mitigated
options.d: Reported to the regulator instead of the client

distractorExplanations.a: Material conflicts must be disclosed proactively.
distractorExplanations.b: Advisers can be paid; the duty is to manage and disclose conflicts.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure goes to clients so they can give informed consent.

options.a: Kept for one year and then destroyed
options.b: Kept for required periods and available
options.c: Kept only for clients with open accounts
options.d: Kept only if a regulator requests them

distractorExplanations.a: Most adviser records must be kept for at least five years.
distractorExplanations.c: Records for closed accounts must still be retained.
distractorExplanations.d: Records must be kept routinely, not only on request.

options.a: Include performance data for any time period
options.b: Contain untrue or misleading material facts
options.c: Mention the adviser's registration status
options.d: Describe the adviser's investment strategy

distractorExplanations.a: Performance can be shown if it meets the rule's conditions.
distractorExplanations.c: Stating registration is allowed if it does not imply endorsement.
distractorExplanations.d: Describing a strategy accurately is permitted.

options.a: The adviser, through lower operating costs
options.b: The broker, through higher trade volume
options.c: The adviser's staff, through perks
options.d: Clients, through research services

distractorExplanations.a: Reducing the adviser's overhead is not the permitted purpose.
distractorExplanations.b: Soft dollars must benefit clients, not generate broker volume.
distractorExplanations.c: Perks for staff fall outside the Section 28(e) safe harbor.

options.a: An exemption from the adviser's fiduciary duty
options.b: SIPC coverage of the adviser's advisory fees
options.c: Qualified custodian, notice, and exam rules
options.d: A shift of supervision from the SEC to FINRA

distractorExplanations.a: Custody adds duties; it never removes fiduciary obligations.
distractorExplanations.b: SIPC protects customer assets at failed broker-dealers, not advisory fees.
distractorExplanations.d: Custody rules come from the Advisers Act; FINRA does not take over.

series-66-readiness-check-ethics-007.explanation: An adviser with custody must keep client assets at a qualified custodian, notify clients, ensure account statements are sent, and in many cases undergo a surprise examination by an independent accountant.

options.a: Best execution
options.b: Soft-dollar research
options.c: Block trade allocation
options.d: Front-running

distractorExplanations.a: Best execution is a duty to clients, not trading ahead of them.
distractorExplanations.b: Soft dollars are research paid for with commissions.
distractorExplanations.c: Block allocation divides combined orders among clients fairly.

options.a: Gives clients disclosures on fees and conflicts
options.b: Registers the adviser's representatives in states
options.c: Reports the adviser's holdings to regulators
options.d: Documents each client's suitability profile

distractorExplanations.b: IAR registration uses Form U4, not the brochure.
distractorExplanations.c: Holdings reports go to regulators on other forms, such as 13F.
distractorExplanations.d: Suitability profiles are client records, not the brochure.

options.a: Acceptable if returns are shown net of fees
options.b: Acceptable if the accounts are clearly named
options.c: Required to show the adviser's top results
options.d: Misleading cherry-picking of results

distractorExplanations.a: Net-of-fee returns do not cure selective presentation.
distractorExplanations.b: Naming the accounts does not fix the omission of the others.
distractorExplanations.c: No rule requires showing only top results.

options.a: Registration of the solicitor as an adviser firm
options.b: Disclosures and a written agreement
options.c: Payment only in cash, not in referral fees
options.d: Approval from each client's custodian

distractorExplanations.a: Solicitors may need to register as IARs in some states, not as adviser firms.
distractorExplanations.c: The rule governs disclosure of compensation, not cash-only payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Custodians are not part of the solicitor arrangement.

options.a: Analyst research reports sent to clients
options.b: Public information that is not yet widely known
options.c: Material nonpublic information in breach of duty
options.d: Rumors discussed on public investment forums

distractorExplanations.a: Research reports sent to clients are not inside information.
distractorExplanations.b: Public information, even if obscure, is not insider information.
distractorExplanations.d: Public rumors are not material nonpublic information from an insider.

options.a: The lowest commission, regardless of execution quality
options.b: Execution through the adviser's affiliated broker
options.c: The fastest execution venue available that day
options.d: The most favorable overall execution reasonably available

distractorExplanations.a: Commission is one factor; best execution weighs total quality.
distractorExplanations.b: An affiliated broker may be used only if it delivers best execution.
distractorExplanations.c: Speed is one factor, not the whole standard.

options.a: Verbal consent after the trade has settled
options.b: Approval from the firm's compliance officer
options.c: A note in the client's annual account review
options.d: Written disclosure and consent before settlement

distractorExplanations.a: Consent must be obtained before completion of the trade and in writing.
distractorExplanations.b: Internal approval does not replace client consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Annual review is too late; consent is needed for each trade.

options.a: Allowed if the loan is repaid within one year
options.b: Prohibited unless the client is a lender
options.c: Allowed if the client signs a promissory note
options.d: Prohibited only for loans above $10,000

distractorExplanations.a: Short repayment does not make borrowing from a retail client acceptable.
distractorExplanations.c: A signed note does not remove the conflict of borrowing from a client.
distractorExplanations.d: NASAA sets no dollar threshold for this prohibition.

series-66-readiness-check-ethics-015.explanation: Under NASAA unethical practice rules, advisers and agents may not borrow from clients unless the client is a broker-dealer, an affiliate, or a financial institution in the business of lending.

options.a: The value of the next-best alternative forgone
options.b: The total cost paid to carry out a decision
options.c: The sunk cost of a past investment decision
options.d: The extra return earned over a benchmark

distractorExplanations.b: Out-of-pocket cost is explicit cost, not opportunity cost.
distractorExplanations.c: Sunk costs are already spent and should not affect decisions.
distractorExplanations.d: Return above a benchmark is alpha.

options.a: Unemployment rises and output falls
options.b: Inflation and interest rates both fall
options.c: Output peaks and then begins to decline
options.d: Unemployment falls and output rises

distractorExplanations.a: Rising unemployment and falling output describe a contraction.
distractorExplanations.b: Inflation and rates usually rise during expansion.
distractorExplanations.c: A peak is the turning point at the end of expansion.

options.a: Rising rates lowering bond prices
options.b: A single company's product recall
options.c: Inflation eroding real returns
options.d: Issuers calling bonds early

distractorExplanations.a: Rate-driven price declines are interest-rate risk.
distractorExplanations.b: A company-specific event is business risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Early calls are call or reinvestment risk.

options.a: Make U.S. exports more competitive abroad
options.b: Make U.S. exports less competitive abroad
options.c: Make imported goods cheaper for U.S. buyers
options.d: Lower returns on foreign stocks for U.S. investors

distractorExplanations.b: A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper abroad, not dearer.
distractorExplanations.c: A weaker dollar makes imports more expensive.
distractorExplanations.d: Foreign returns rise in dollar terms when the dollar weakens.

options.a: Fewer bank reserves and higher short-term rates
options.b: More bank reserves and lower short-term rates
options.c: Higher reserve requirements for member banks
options.d: A higher discount rate charged to member banks

distractorExplanations.a: Selling Treasuries drains reserves; buying adds them.
distractorExplanations.c: Reserve requirements are a separate tool, and are currently zero.
distractorExplanations.d: The discount rate is set separately from open-market operations.

options.a: Building permits and new orders
options.b: Consumer price index changes
options.c: Average duration of unemployment
options.d: Personal income and industrial output

distractorExplanations.b: CPI is a lagging indicator.
distractorExplanations.c: Duration of unemployment is lagging.
distractorExplanations.d: Personal income and industrial production are coincident indicators.

series-66-readiness-check-state-law-008.prompt: Which is an example of a leading economic indicator?

options.a: Falling prices combined with slow growth
options.b: Stagnant growth with high inflation
options.c: Strong growth with rising inflation
options.d: Falling unemployment with low inflation

distractorExplanations.a: Falling prices with weak growth describe deflation.
distractorExplanations.c: Strong growth with rising inflation is an overheating expansion.
distractorExplanations.d: Low unemployment and low inflation describe a healthy expansion.

options.a: The time to receipt gets longer
options.b: The discount rate decreases
options.c: The discount rate increases
options.d: Inflation expectations rise

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting longer lowers present value.
distractorExplanations.c: A higher discount rate lowers present value.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher inflation expectations usually raise discount rates and lower present value.

options.a: Risk specific to one company or its industry sector
options.b: Risk that an issuer fails to pay interest or principal
options.c: Market-wide risk that diversification cannot remove
options.d: Risk that a security cannot be sold quickly

distractorExplanations.a: Company or industry risk is unsystematic and can be diversified.
distractorExplanations.b: Failure to pay is credit (default) risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Difficulty selling is liquidity risk.

options.a: Moved about 20% less than the market
options.b: Returned 1.2% more than the market each year
options.c: Had 20% lower volatility than its peers
options.d: Moved about 20% more than the market

distractorExplanations.a: A beta below 1 moves less than the market.
distractorExplanations.b: Beta measures relative movement, not excess return.
distractorExplanations.c: Beta compares a stock to the market, not to peer volatility.

options.a: Open-market operations
options.b: Changes to the discount rate
options.c: Government spending and taxation
options.d: Changes to reserve requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Open-market operations are monetary policy run by the Fed.
distractorExplanations.b: The discount rate is a Federal Reserve tool.
distractorExplanations.d: Reserve requirements are set by the Fed.

options.a: Price changes that producers receive for goods
options.b: Price changes for a basket of consumer goods
options.c: Total value of goods and services produced
options.d: Changes in wages paid across the economy

distractorExplanations.a: Prices received by producers are measured by the PPI.
distractorExplanations.c: Total output is GDP.
distractorExplanations.d: Wage growth is measured by employment cost data.

options.a: A sign that inflation is accelerating
options.b: A sign that long-term rates will rise
options.c: A possible recession warning signal
options.d: A sign of strong economic expansion

distractorExplanations.a: Inversion often reflects expected slowing, not rising inflation.
distractorExplanations.b: Inversion means long rates sit below short rates, often expecting cuts.
distractorExplanations.d: Strong expansions usually have normal, upward-sloping curves.

options.a: Has an active manager who trades the portfolio
options.b: Continuously issues new units like an open-end fund
options.c: Trades intraday on exchanges at market prices
options.d: Has a fixed portfolio and a termination date

distractorExplanations.a: UITs are unmanaged; the portfolio is fixed.
distractorExplanations.b: UITs issue units once in a primary offering.
distractorExplanations.c: Most UIT units are redeemed with the sponsor, not traded intraday.

options.a: Invested in separate account subaccounts
options.b: Held in the insurer's general account
options.c: Credited with a fixed rate set each year
options.d: Linked to an index with a guaranteed floor

distractorExplanations.b: General account assets back whole life, which has guaranteed values.
distractorExplanations.c: A declared annual rate describes universal life.
distractorExplanations.d: Index-linked credits with a floor describe indexed life.

options.a: Sell shares back to the company at market price
options.b: Buy more shares, often at a discount, pro rata
options.c: Receive new shares free as a stock dividend
options.d: Convert common shares into preferred stock

distractorExplanations.a: Selling back to the company is a tender offer or buyback.
distractorExplanations.c: Free shares are a stock dividend, not a rights offering.
distractorExplanations.d: Conversion features belong to convertible securities.

options.a: Revenues from the financed project
options.b: Lease payments from a public agency
options.c: The taxing power of the issuer
options.d: Federal guarantees on the principal

distractorExplanations.a: Project revenues back revenue bonds.
distractorExplanations.b: Lease payments back lease-rental bonds.
distractorExplanations.d: Municipal bonds are not federally guaranteed.

options.a: Raises the company's total market value
options.b: Lowers share count and raises share price
options.c: Changes each holder's percentage ownership
options.d: Raises share count, lowers price, same value

distractorExplanations.a: A split does not change the company's total value.
distractorExplanations.b: Fewer shares at a higher price describe a reverse split.
distractorExplanations.c: Every holder gets proportional shares, so ownership percentages stay the same.

options.a: Issued by the company, often with long terms
options.b: Standardized contracts cleared by the OCC
options.c: Created by investors writing contracts
options.d: Rights to sell stock at a set price

distractorExplanations.b: OCC-cleared standardized contracts are listed options.
distractorExplanations.c: Options are written by investors; warrants come from the issuer.
distractorExplanations.d: Warrants are rights to buy, not sell.

options.a: Voting rights equal to common stockholders
options.b: Extra dividends tied to common dividends
options.c: Unpaid dividends that accumulate over time
options.d: The right to convert into common shares

distractorExplanations.a: Participation relates to dividends, not voting.
distractorExplanations.c: Accumulating unpaid dividends describes cumulative preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: Conversion rights describe convertible preferred.

options.a: The credit rating of the mortgage servicer
options.b: The coupon rate on the underlying mortgages
options.c: Prepayment speed and the tranche's priority
options.d: The number of tranches in the CMO structure

distractorExplanations.a: Servicer ratings matter little to tranche risk.
distractorExplanations.b: The coupon matters less than how prepayments are allocated.
distractorExplanations.d: Tranche count alone does not define a tranche's risk.

options.a: Tracking error from holding the index stocks
options.b: Daily NAV pricing instead of market pricing
options.c: SIPC protection against market losses
options.d: Issuer credit risk plus index risk

distractorExplanations.a: ETNs hold no stocks; they are unsecured debt.
distractorExplanations.b: ETNs trade intraday at market prices.
distractorExplanations.c: SIPC never covers market losses.

options.a: Buy-and-hold investors unfamiliar with compounding
options.b: Day traders who monitor positions during the day
options.c: Traders using it briefly with a clear strategy
options.d: Institutions hedging short-term index exposure

distractorExplanations.b: Active intraday users are the intended audience.
distractorExplanations.c: Short-term tactical use with understanding fits the design.
distractorExplanations.d: Short-term institutional hedging matches the daily reset.

options.a: Full upside with no issuer credit risk
options.b: Caps, buffers, or participation rates
options.c: FDIC insurance on the note's principal
options.d: Dividends paid from the index stocks

distractorExplanations.a: Structured notes carry the issuer's credit risk and often cap gains.
